new_en: (There) This is understandable when one hires the non-Jew as a contractor, or leases it to the non-Jew for a month or half a month; he receives it. This is the correct reading.

(There) And even rendering a utensil unusable, and everything is permitted in a case of monetary loss. This is the correct reading. Note: See my sefer, page 18a, where I concluded that those who prohibit are more numerous than those who permit, and we do not rule in accordance with this law; see there.

(In Magen Avraham, seif katan 5.) What he wrote in Hagahot Ashiri there represents another view. Everyone agrees here that if he designated it, it has the status of a utensil, as stated above. Note: Meaning, according to the Rif, in any event it is permitted only for use of the utensil itself or use of its place. According to Rabbeinu Chananel, however, who compares it to implements used for weaving and pressing, even moving it for use of its place is forbidden.
(There) For he separates only from that which is adjacent. Note: See Bach, who explains that this passage belongs earlier than the present one; see there.
(There) And see the Rosh in the name of Baal HaIttur. This is the correct reading.

[7] In an unusual manner, etc. Mordechai's wording is that kneading by means of a shinui is permitted. This implies that according to those who prohibit in siman 324, seif 3, it would likewise be forbidden here. It is possible, however, that here everyone agrees it is permitted, since he does not pour water onto them, but rather takes them with wet hands (Magen Avraham). This is contrary to Levush, who wrote that he pours water over them, etc. It is possible that because this is not done in a vessel in which the water remains, it is considered as though he is not pouring water onto them. Nevertheless, it appears to me that even aside from this, everyone agrees it is permitted, as explained in siman 321, seif 16. [8] His hands with salt, etc. Taz raised a difficulty from bran, where doing it in an unusual manner is permitted, and he strained to resolve it. There is no difficulty, because kneading performed with a shinui is not considered kneading, whereas creating a new entity is different.

[2] It is permitted to say, etc. Nachalat Tzvi questioned this from siman 307, seif 5, where a rabbinic prohibition was permitted only in a matter that is itself rabbinic and for the sake of a mitzvah. In my humble opinion there is no difficulty, because this case is different, as Mordechai explains at the end of chapter Bameh Behemah: if he is not permitted to do so, he may come to perform the act himself. Taz cites this reason and writes that accordingly the earlier ruling, that one may make the animal run, cannot refer to a case where he fears it may die, and therefore they did not act stringently there. This is puzzling. On the contrary, if he does not fear that it may die there would be greater reason for stringency, because he is not panicked and will not perform a Torah prohibition himself. Perhaps there is a scribal error in his words, and the matter requires study. Moreover, the Tosefta at the end of chapter 17 explicitly states that there is concern that the animal may die.

[4] Wheat, etc. Malbushei Yom Tov writes in the name of Derishot Maharash that it is forbidden to rub a bottle with oats called haverin. Mahari Weil writes that it is permitted to throw something across the table, contrary to those who say it is forbidden because one thereby throws away the angel.

[7] A deaf person and an incompetent person, etc. The deaf person referred to here is one who speaks but does not hear. One who neither hears nor speaks does not join the zimun, as stated above in siman 55, seif 8, and so writes Lechem Chamudot. Likewise, this does not refer to the halachic category of an incompetent person discussed by the Sages, as explained in Yoreh De'ah, siman 1, but to one who is not wise and whom people regard as mentally incompetent. In Eliyah Rabbah on Yoreh De'ah this will be explained at length. [8] See Yoreh De'ah, siman 334, and above, siman 55, seif 12.

(1) Wadding. Meaning dry wadding, as stated in siman 257, seif 3. (2) On an occasional basis. This excludes one who regularly uses it for insulation, in which case it loses its status of muktzeh even without an explicit designation. Bach holds that even doing so twice is sufficient. (3) It is forbidden to move them. Ordinarily they are valuable and a person sets them aside because they are intended for making felt. They are therefore muktzeh machmat chisaron kis, since he is particular not to use them for other purposes. Consequently, even if he insulated with them only on an occasional basis, they remain set aside and do not become subordinate to the insulation. (4) Some of them are exposed. This leaves a free place by which to grasp the cover, so that he will not have to move the wadding directly. (5) If he designated them for this. Meaning, he designated them before Shabbos permanently for insulation. Even designation by thought alone, without verbalizing it, is sufficient. (6) But if he insulated, etc. Although ordinary wool shearings are muktzeh because they are intended for spinning and weaving, they are not as important as wadding. Once he insulated with them, it is as though he designated them for this purpose. (7) For merchandise. Since he holds them as merchandise, he presumably intends to return them afterward to storage. He therefore does not subordinate them to the insulation, and they remain muktzeh unless he designated them for insulation before Shabbos. (8) That he takes the cover, etc. This refers to a case where some of it is exposed, as explained above regarding wadding. If none of it is exposed, he may insert a spindle and shake off the cover, as stated below in siman 311, seif 9. (9) For it did not become a base. The cover does not serve the wool. On the contrary, the wool serves the pot by warming it.

To hold. See Taz, who writes that the concern is degradation of Yom Tov. See siman 522, for on Yom Tov the prohibition of carrying does not apply in the same manner because of the principle that an act permitted for food preparation is also permitted for another Yom Tov need. Thus the concern is mainly weekday-like conduct, and it applies in a public domain or karmelit where many people are found. On Shabbos, however, there is also the issue of carrying outside an eruv. Levush gives the reason that perhaps he may come to carry the item 4 amot in a public domain, since he is capable of walking without it. A practical difference arises where he already went out into the public domain. Magen Avraham, seif katan 25, in the name of Eliyah Rabbah, writes that where the entire concern is lest he carry 4 amot, if he already went out he need not remove it there. Where the issue is carrying a burden, however, he must remove it. See Shabbos 66a, Rashi and Tosafos there. Regarding a cane with a nail at its end that certainly makes a hole as one walks, this is a psik reisha, though he has no benefit from it. Where he walks on unpaved ground, one may consider whether the hole is of no use to him and the prohibition is rabbinic. A psik reisha in a rabbinic prohibition from which he derives no benefit may perhaps be permitted. I discussed this at length in my novellae to Shabbos 66a. See Magen Avraham, siman 314, seif katan 5, who discusses psik reisha and shows that even in a rabbinic prohibition it is forbidden, as is evident in siman 337 regarding dragging a bench when this will certainly make a furrow. The case of a psik reisha from which he derives no benefit means that he truly has no benefit from it. Accordingly, I do not see a clear basis to permit a cane with a nail that certainly makes a hole. One might nevertheless argue that it is destructive in the public domain, is digging in an unusual manner, and involves other grounds for leniency. The matter requires study; see Magen Avraham, simanim 314 and 337. The Tur cites the ruling in Beitzah 25b that a person may be carried in a chair on Shabbos if the public needs him. The Mechaber omitted it here and recorded it in siman 522 regarding Yom Tov. Here, in a public domain, there can be a Torah prohibition, while a karmelit was prohibited lest one come to a public domain. Although a living person carries himself and the bed is secondary to him, and the Sages did not decree in the usual case, the Mechaber nevertheless omitted the leniency on Shabbos. It may be that Yom Tov is different because there is no Torah-level carrying concern in this context, only weekday-like conduct, and where the public needs the person there is no such concern, particularly for the honor of Torah. On Shabbos, however, the activity remains within the framework of melacha and was prohibited even where the immediate prohibition is rabbinic. Rama also omitted this leniency, which indicates that he agrees. It is possible that even through a non-Jew it is forbidden in a public domain, since the Sages attached this prohibition to a Scriptural verse, as Beit Yosef explains in siman 244. Yet according to those who permit a double rabbinic prohibition for a mitzvah, one may argue that where the public needs someone for Torah study, carrying him through a non-Jew is permitted, since a living person carries himself. Bach writes that it is permitted even on Shabbos because the prohibition is rabbinic. The practice in some places of seating the sandak together with the infant on a chair and having Jews carry them to the synagogue on Shabbos is certainly forbidden even in a karmelit. The infant is not secondary to the sandak, and in a public domain one would be liable for carrying him. See Magen Avraham, siman 308, seif katan 71; siman 331, seif katan 5; and Taz, siman 266, seif katan 4, regarding carrying through a non-Jew where our public domains are treated as a karmelit.

And some prohibit. See Taz and Eliyah Rabbah, letter 64. I have already written above that where the custom is to wear an under-gartel and an over-gartel, meaning that one is unattractive and the second is attractive, and they do so in order that it be proper to gird the second over the first, or where the second is short, it is certainly permitted. He writes there in the name of Sefer HaTerumah and Maharam that even according to the opinion prohibiting 2 belts, the prohibition is only rabbinic; see there. See also letter 14, that the same applies where he makes a bow, so that it functions as a long belt, like a sash; see there. See Tosafos, Shabbos 59b, s.v. Trei Hemayni. Where there is benefit and this is the normal manner, a case such as ours is permitted. Tosafos there were troubled by the case of a fire and did not answer that the Sages permitted a rabbinic prohibition because of monetary loss. At first glance this would indicate that they understood the prohibition to be Torah-level. This is not so, for in a case of loss they permitted moving muktzeh, but not carrying out even where the latter is only rabbinic. See siman 334, where this will be explained.

Hat. See Taz, who discusses Shabbos 138b and Eruvin 102b. Each interpretation there yields both a leniency and a stringency. According to Rashi, the leniency is that when the hat is firmly secured with a strap, or when it is not normal for the wearer to go bareheaded, it is permitted even if the brim forms a tefach of overhang. For this reason, extending a cloak a tefach beyond one's head is permitted. The rationale is that making a temporary tent is rabbinic and, in a case of this sort, since the covering is upon his head, it is not treated as a tent; alternatively, there is no tent without partitions. See Taz, siman 315, letter 8. If, however, the cloak extends from his head with a tefach-wide roof and hangs in front of him, it constitutes a genuine temporary tent with roof and partitions, so the first rationale must be relied upon. Rashi's stringency is that where the hat is not secured it is forbidden because it may fall and he may carry it 4 amot in a public domain, even if it bends, even if there is no tefach, and even if it was already on his head before Shabbos. According to Rabbeinu Chananel and Rabbeinu Tam, however, when there is no tefach the matter is permitted and we are not concerned at all that it may fall and be carried. Bach explains likewise. Their stringency is that where there is a tefach of stiff brim it may be forbidden as a temporary tent even when firmly secured. The Mechaber in seif 40 follows Rabbeinu Chananel, Rabbeinu Tam, and Rambam, chapter 22 of the Laws of Shabbos, law 14. The Rif's text contains the word 'rather,' and it is possible that Rambam does not disagree with his teacher. The discussion can be read as follows: a sayana is a felt hat. If its brim is a tefach it is forbidden; if it is less than a tefach it is permitted. The novelty in the latter ruling is that we do not fear that it will fall and be carried, even though felt does not sit perfectly on the head. The Gemara then retracts that assumption and concludes that concern for falling does exist, while the distinction concerns whether the brim is sufficiently stiff and roof-like to constitute a temporary tent. This also accords with Rambam's wording that the brim must be extremely stiff like a roof. Accordingly, there is no contradiction in the Mechaber: although in seif 40 he follows the view that the prohibition depends upon a tefach-wide roof, in seif 41 he nevertheless records and rules like the opinion that we fear the hat may fall and be carried 4 amot in a public domain. Taz distinguishes between our Britel and a Kapelush. In a Britel it is not defined which part serves as a tent and which as a head covering, and the wearer intends only a head covering, so it is permitted according to Rabbeinu Chananel. A Kapelush, or what is called a Hut, whose brim extends a tefach around the head and is very stiff, may be forbidden according to Rabbeinu Tam. Where such hats are folded into a triangular shield shape, it is possible that their width is less than a tefach. Even if they project a tefach from the head, both length and a tefach of width are required; this will be discussed in siman 315. A Britel is nevertheless forbidden outside an eruv according to Rashi, because it may fall and one may carry it 4 amot in a public domain or karmelit; see siman 303, seif 18. Nachalat Tzvi writes that in a karmelit, which is a rabbinic doubt, one may rely on Rabbeinu Tam and Rabbeinu Chananel. According to the Mechaber, however, who incorporates both concerns, and because we frequently find a decree lest an item fall and be carried 4 amot in a public domain, Taz's ruling appears correct that outside an eruv it should be prohibited. It requires study what people rely upon to be lenient. The Gemara did not distinguish between an obvious brim such as that of a Hut or Kapelush and our less distinct Britel, perhaps because the form of sayana itself had a recognizable brim. Taz's statement that the Mechaber was lenient in seif 41 where one went out wearing it before Shabbos applies likewise where there is no tefach or the brim bends; he mentions 1 of the alternatives. Regarding the pantines and the ruling in seif 7 that a minor may not go out wearing a shoe too large for him, although it is not normal to walk barefoot, one can answer that because the oversized shoe is difficult to walk in, there is greater concern that it will fall and he will carry it 4 amot in a public domain, as explained above.

One should make the hole along the length of the tallis, no higher than 3 fingerbreadths, meaning thumbbreadths, from the corner (Kol Bo, siman 22; Maimoniyot; Hagahot Semak, siman 31), because above that point it is not called the corner; and no lower than the measure from the thumb joint to the end of the nail, because the verse says 'upon the corner,' and if it were lower than a full thumb joint it would be beneath the corner. {Rama: This measurement is taken in a straight line from the corner, not diagonally (Beit Yosef).}

One who put food or drink into his mouth without a blessing. It contains 2 seifim: If one forgot and put liquid into his mouth without reciting a blessing, he swallows it and does not recite the preceding blessing over it. {Rama: Some say that he does recite a blessing over it, and this appears to be the primary ruling. [Rashba in the name of Ra'avad; Rosh, chapter 3 of Sheloshah SheAchlu; and Rambam, chapter 8 of the Laws of Blessings].}

Seif katan 4, it is a doubt, etc., whether the sea, etc. Tiberias was surrounded by a wall from the days of Yehoshua bin Nun, except that on 1 side the sea formed its wall. The Gemara was uncertain whether the advantage of a wall causes the city to be judged as a walled city because the wall protects it from enemies, in which case the sea too is called a wall, since it likewise protects; or whether the function of the wall is that it conceals the city's inhabitants from the enemy's sight so that they can hide themselves in a concealed place, which the sea does not do because it leaves them exposed and they cannot hide. According to the latter understanding, the sea does not have the legal status of a wall.
